summary:
Arunāchal Pradesh stands under India's national framework on gender recognition, criminal law and police conduct, and that framework is what a trans visitor to the state should be assessed against. Parliament of India passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the self-identification route in the 2019 law.

Recognition is now limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex persons, and requires medical certification. Medical boards and district authorities certify whether gender-affirming surgery has been performed. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. The amendment reverses the position set by the Supreme Court of India's 2014 ruling on gender identity.

The amendment also creates offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender. Human Rights Watch warned on 26 March 2026 that this provision could be used against support networks around trans people.

Coverage of identity documentation is thin. Of 487,803 transgender persons recorded in the census, about 32,500 hold identity cards; the wider estimate of transgender people in India is around two million. Presidential assent was still pending in late March 2026, when Human Rights Watch urged the president not to sign the bill, and a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw it, calling removal of self-identification a setback against the 2014 ruling.

The government presents the narrower definition as a way of targeting welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection to those it recognises. Critics, including rights activists such as Akkai Padmashali, state that the amendment criminalises trans existence and excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

The baseline on entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court of India in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, Central Industrial Security Force personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.
tangentialFactors:
Two figures for the trans population circulate and do not reconcile: 487,803 persons recorded in the census against an estimate of around two million. The gap suggests a large share of trans people in India are not counted, which bears on how visible a trans visitor is likely to be in official encounters.

Documentation coverage is low relative to the recognised population. Roughly 32,500 of the 487,803 census-recorded transgender persons hold identity cards, so identity documents certifying gender status are not a common artifact a visitor can rely on.

The legal position was in flux at the time of writing. The March 2026 amendment had passed both houses of Parliament but presidential assent was still pending in late March 2026, and a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel had asked the government to withdraw it. Whether the bill was subsequently assented to is not resolved in these sources.

The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 places police abuse of LGBT+ people outside systemic classification and likelier in conservative rural areas. Arunāchal Pradesh is largely rural and administratively remote, which places it closer to the environment the note flags as higher-risk than to the metropolitan settings where most documented checkpoint incidents occurred.

Documented friction clusters on transport and aviation security rather than on immigration control as such: railway stations in 2024, an international airport terminal in November 2024, and passport medical examinations challenged in February 2026. Inter-state travel within India therefore carries more exposure than arrival formalities alone.

Residents seeking legal recognition must now satisfy medical certification, with medical boards and district authorities certifying whether gender-affirming surgery has taken place. Recognition under the 2019 law's self-identification route is no longer available to those outside the historically recognised groups and intersex persons.

Identity documentation is issued to a small minority of the transgender population. Around 32,500 of the 487,803 census-recorded transgender persons hold identity cards, so most residents live without a document evidencing their recognised gender.

The government's stated purpose for the narrower definition is to direct welfare schemes and anti-trafficking protection to recognised groups. Residents who self-identify as trans men, trans women or non-binary outside those groups are outside the scheme and outside the amendment's protections.

The amendment creates an offence, punishable with up to life imprisonment, for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender. Human Rights Watch's assessment is that the provision risks being turned against support networks that assist trans people.

Sexual-violence protection changed in 2024. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code without carrying over the gender-identity-specific offences, and trans residents report fear of increased assault under the new code.

Same-sex marriage and civil partnership remain unavailable to residents, although courts have treated same-sex couples as family units in other contexts. Discrimination on grounds including sex, read to cover gender identity, is barred.

Police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy were directed by the Madras High Court in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police on 7 June 2021, with further directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. These are national obligations rather than measures specific to Arunāchal Pradesh.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory concerns Arunāchal Pradesh directly. State-level police practice, the presence or absence of facilities that accommodate trans visitors, and any local orders of the Government of Arunāchal Pradesh are unresolved and not sourced here.

Whether the March 2026 amendment received presidential assent after late March 2026 is unresolved; the inventory records the bill as passed and assent as pending.

The relationship between the census figure of 487,803 and the estimate of around two million transgender people in India is not explained by any source here.

Whether the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita's removal of gender-identity-specific offences has produced a measurable change in charging or conviction outcomes is not sourced; the inventory records community fear of increased assault, not enforcement statistics.

The Madras High Court guidelines and the Allahabad High Court relief order bind in their own jurisdictions. Their application by police and passport authorities in Arunāchal Pradesh is not addressed in the inventory.

The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 is a bilateral assessment of India as a whole and does not break out individual states.
